title: The Cross Product
lead: The cross product of two vectors in space is a third vector orthogonal to both. This section computes it from components and by a determinant, finds its direction by the right-hand rule and its length from the angle between the factors, and uses it for areas, volumes of parallelepipeds and torque.
objectives: Calculate the cross product of two given vectors.
Use determinants to calculate a cross product.
Find a vector orthogonal to two given vectors.
Determine areas and volumes by using the cross product.
Calculate the torque of a given force and position vector.
summary_html:
• The cross product $\kvecu\;\times \;\kvecv $ of two vectors $\kvecu=\langle u_{1},u_{2},u_{3}\rangle$ and $\kvecv=\langle v_{1},v_{2},v_{3}\rangle$ is a vector orthogonal to both $\kvecu $ and $\kvecv.$ Its length is given by $\| \kvecu\;\times \;\kvecv\| =\| \kvecu\| \cdot \| \kvecv\| \cdot \sin \ktheta ,$ where $\ktheta$ is the angle between $\kvecu $ and $\kvecv.$ Its direction is given by the right-hand rule.
  • The algebraic formula for calculating the cross product of two vectors, $\kvecu=\langle u_{1},u_{2},u_{3}\rangle \;\text{and}\;\kvecv=\langle v_{1},v_{2},v_{3}\rangle ,$ is $\kvecu\;\times \;\kvecv=(u_{2}v_{3}-u_{3}v_{2})\kveci-(u_{1}v_{3}-u_{3}v_{1})\kvecj+(u_{1}v_{2}-u_{2}v_{1})\kveck.$
  • The cross product satisfies the following properties for vectors $\kvecu,\kvecv,\;\text{and}\;\kvecw,$ and scalar $c\text{:}$
  • $\kvecu\;\times \;\kvecv=-(\kvecv\;\times \;\kvecu)$
  • $\kvecu\;\times \;(\kvecv+\kvecw)=\kvecu\;\times \;\kvecv+\kvecu\;\times \;\kvecw $
  • $c(\kvecu\;\times \;\kvecv)=(c\kvecu)\;\times \;\kvecv=\kvecu\;\times \;(c\kvecv)$
  • $\kvecu\;\times \;\kveczero=\kveczero\;\times \;\kvecu=\kveczero$
  • $\kvecv\;\times \;\kvecv=0$
  • $\kvecu\cdot (\kvecv\;\times \;\kvecw)=(\kvecu\;\times \;\kvecv)\cdot \kvecw $
  • The cross product of vectors $\kvecu=\langle u_{1},u_{2},u_{3}\rangle$ and $\kvecv=\langle v_{1},v_{2},v_{3}\rangle$ is the determinant $\left|\begin{array}{lll}\kveci & \kvecj & \kveck \\ u_{1} & u_{2} & u_{3} \\ v_{1} & v_{2} & v_{3}\end{array}\right|.$
  • If vectors $\kvecu $ and $\kvecv $ form adjacent sides of a parallelogram, then the area of the parallelogram is given by $\| \kvecu\;\times \;\kvecv\| .$
  • The triple scalar product of vectors $\kvecu,$ $\kvecv,$ and $\kvecw $ is $\kvecu\cdot (\kvecv\;\times \;\kvecw).$
  • The volume of a parallelepiped with adjacent edges given by vectors $\kvecu,\kvecv,\;\text{and}\;\kvecw $ is $V=|\kvecu\cdot (\kvecv\;\times \;\kvecw)|.$
  • If the triple scalar product of vectors $\kvecu,\kvecv,\;\text{and}\;\kvecw $ is zero, then the vectors are coplanar. The converse is also true: If the vectors are coplanar, then their triple scalar product is zero.
  • The cross product can be used to identify a vector orthogonal to two given vectors or to a plane.
  • Torque $\ktau$ measures the tendency of a force to produce rotation about an axis of rotation. If force $\kvecF $ is acting at a distance $\kvecr $ from the axis, then torque is equal to the cross product of $\kvecr $ and $\kvecF\text{:}$ $\ktau=\kvecr\;\times \;\kvecF.$

Determine the real number $\alpha$ such that $\textbf{u}\;\times \;\textbf{v}$ and $\textbf{i}$ are orthogonal, where $\textbf{u}=3\textbf{i}+\textbf{j}-5\textbf{k}$ and $\textbf{v}=4\textbf{i}-2\textbf{j}+\alpha \textbf{k}.$

Show that $\textbf{u}\;\times \;\textbf{v}$ and $2\textbf{i}-14\textbf{j}+2\textbf{k}$ cannot be orthogonal for any $\alpha$ real number, where $\textbf{u}=\textbf{i}+7\textbf{j}-\textbf{k}$ and $\textbf{v}=\alpha \textbf{i}+5\textbf{j}+\textbf{k}.$

answer.solution: By the definition of the cross product, $\mathbf{u}\times\mathbf{v}=\langle 7(1)-(-1)(5),\,-(1(1)-(-1)\alpha),\,1(5)-7\alpha\rangle=\langle 12,\,-1-\alpha,\,5-7\alpha\rangle.$ Its dot product with $\langle 2,-14,2\rangle$ is $24+14(1+\alpha)+10-14\alpha=48,$ which is never 0. So for no real $\alpha$ are the two vectors orthogonal.

exercises.prompt: Show that $\textbf{u}\;\times \;\textbf{v}$ is orthogonal to $\textbf{u}+\textbf{v}$ and $\textbf{u}-\textbf{v},$ where $\textbf{u}$ and $\textbf{v}$ are nonzero vectors.

answer.solution: The cross product $\mathbf{u}\times\mathbf{v}$ is orthogonal to both $\mathbf{u}$ and $\mathbf{v},$ so $(\mathbf{u}\times\mathbf{v})\cdot\mathbf{u}=0$ and $(\mathbf{u}\times\mathbf{v})\cdot\mathbf{v}=0.$ By the distributive property of the dot product, $(\mathbf{u}\times\mathbf{v})\cdot(\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v})=0+0=0$ and $(\mathbf{u}\times\mathbf{v})\cdot(\mathbf{u}-\mathbf{v})=0-0=0,$ so $\mathbf{u}\times\mathbf{v}$ is orthogonal to $\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v}$ and to $\mathbf{u}-\mathbf{v}.$

exercises.prompt: Show that $\textbf{v}\;\times \;\textbf{u}$ is orthogonal to $(\textbf{u}\cdot \textbf{v})(\textbf{u}+\textbf{v})+\text{u},$ where $\textbf{u}$ and $\textbf{v}$ are nonzero vectors.

answer.solution: $\mathbf{v}\times\mathbf{u}$ is orthogonal to $\mathbf{u}$ and to $\mathbf{v},$ so its dot product with each is 0. Writing $c=\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v},$ a scalar, $(\mathbf{v}\times\mathbf{u})\cdot(c(\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v})+\mathbf{u})=c\,(\mathbf{v}\times\mathbf{u})\cdot\mathbf{u}+c\,(\mathbf{v}\times\mathbf{u})\cdot\mathbf{v}+(\mathbf{v}\times\mathbf{u})\cdot\mathbf{u}=0+0+0=0,$ so the two vectors are orthogonal.

Use the sine and cosine of the angle between two nonzero vectors $\textbf{u}$ and $\textbf{v}$ to prove Lagrange’s identity: ${\| \textbf{u}\;\times \;\textbf{v}\|}^{2}={\| \textbf{u}\|}^{2}{\| \textbf{v}\|}^{2}-{(\textbf{u}\cdot \textbf{v})}^{2}.$

answer.solution: Let $\theta$ be the angle between $\mathbf{u}$ and $\mathbf{v}.$ Then $\|\mathbf{u}\times\mathbf{v}\|=\|\mathbf{u}\|\|\mathbf{v}\|\sin\theta$ and $\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}=\|\mathbf{u}\|\|\mathbf{v}\|\cos\theta.$ Squaring the first and using $\sin^{2}\theta=1-\cos^{2}\theta,$ $\|\mathbf{u}\times\mathbf{v}\|^{2}=\|\mathbf{u}\|^{2}\|\mathbf{v}\|^{2}(1-\cos^{2}\theta)=\|\mathbf{u}\|^{2}\|\mathbf{v}\|^{2}-(\|\mathbf{u}\|\|\mathbf{v}\|\cos\theta)^{2}=\|\mathbf{u}\|^{2}\|\mathbf{v}\|^{2}-(\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v})^{2}.$

exercises.prompt: Nonzero vectors $\textbf{u}$ and $\textbf{v}$ are called collinear if there exists a nonzero scalar $\alpha$ such that $\textbf{v}=\alpha \textbf{u}.$ Show that $\textbf{u}$ and $\textbf{v}$ are collinear if and only if $\textbf{u}\;\times \;\textbf{v}=\mathbf{0}.$

answer.solution: If $\mathbf{v}=\alpha\mathbf{u},$ then $\mathbf{u}\times\mathbf{v}=\alpha(\mathbf{u}\times\mathbf{u})=\alpha\mathbf{0}=\mathbf{0}.$ Conversely, if $\mathbf{u}\times\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{0},$ then $\|\mathbf{u}\|\|\mathbf{v}\|\sin\theta=0;$ the vectors are nonzero, so $\sin\theta=0$ and $\theta=0$ or $\pi:$ $\mathbf{v}$ has the same or the opposite direction as $\mathbf{u},$ so $\mathbf{v}=\alpha\mathbf{u}$ with $\alpha=\pm\frac{\|\mathbf{v}\|}{\|\mathbf{u}\|}\ne 0,$ and the vectors are collinear.

exercises.prompt: Nonzero vectors $\textbf{u}$ and $\textbf{v}$ are called collinear if there exists a nonzero scalar $\alpha$ such that $\textbf{v}=\alpha \textbf{u}.$ Show that vectors $\kAB$ and $\kAC$ are collinear, where $A(4,1,0),$ $B(6,5,-2),$ and $C(5,3,-1).$

answer.solution: $\kAB=\langle 6-4,5-1,-2-0\rangle=\langle 2,4,-2\rangle$ and $\kAC=\langle 5-4,3-1,-1-0\rangle=\langle 1,2,-1\rangle.$ So $\kAB=2\kAC$ with the nonzero scalar 2, and the vectors are collinear; equivalently $\kAB\times\kAC=\langle 4(-1)-(-2)(2),\,-(2(-1)-(-2)(1)),\,2(2)-4(1)\rangle=\mathbf{0}.$

exercises.prompt:
Let $\textbf{u},\textbf{v},\;\text{and}\;\textbf{w}$ be three-dimensional vectors and $c$ be a real number. Prove the following properties of the cross product.

a. $\textbf{u}\;\times \;\textbf{u}=\mathbf{0}$

b. $\textbf{u}\;\times \;(\textbf{v}+\textbf{w})=(\textbf{u}\;\times \;\textbf{v})+(\textbf{u}\;\times \;\textbf{w})$

c. $c(\textbf{u}\;\times \;\textbf{v})=(c\textbf{u})\;\times \;\textbf{v}=\textbf{u}\;\times \;(c\textbf{v})$

d. $\textbf{u}\cdot \mathbf{(}\textbf{u}\;\times \;\textbf{v}\mathbf{)=0}$

answer.solution:
Let $\mathbf{u}=\langle u_{1},u_{2},u_{3}\rangle,$ $\mathbf{v}=\langle v_{1},v_{2},v_{3}\rangle,$ $\mathbf{w}=\langle w_{1},w_{2},w_{3}\rangle.$

a. $\mathbf{u}\times\mathbf{u}=\langle u_{2}u_{3}-u_{3}u_{2},\,-(u_{1}u_{3}-u_{3}u_{1}),\,u_{1}u_{2}-u_{2}u_{1}\rangle=\langle 0,0,0\rangle=\mathbf{0}.$

b. The first component of $\mathbf{u}\times(\mathbf{v}+\mathbf{w})$ is $u_{2}(v_{3}+w_{3})-u_{3}(v_{2}+w_{2})=(u_{2}v_{3}-u_{3}v_{2})+(u_{2}w_{3}-u_{3}w_{2}),$ the sum of the first components of $\mathbf{u}\times\mathbf{v}$ and $\mathbf{u}\times\mathbf{w};$ the second and third components split the same way.

c. Each component of $\mathbf{u}\times\mathbf{v}$ is a difference of products with one factor from $\mathbf{u}$ and one from $\mathbf{v};$ replacing $\mathbf{u}$ by $c\mathbf{u},$ or $\mathbf{v}$ by $c\mathbf{v},$ multiplies every such product, and so every component, by $c.$ Hence $c(\mathbf{u}\times\mathbf{v})=(c\mathbf{u})\times\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{u}\times(c\mathbf{v}).$

d. $\mathbf{u}\cdot(\mathbf{u}\times\mathbf{v})=u_{1}(u_{2}v_{3}-u_{3}v_{2})+u_{2}(u_{3}v_{1}-u_{1}v_{3})+u_{3}(u_{1}v_{2}-u_{2}v_{1}),$ and the six terms cancel in pairs, leaving 0.

exercises.prompt: Nonzero vectors $\textbf{u},\textbf{v},\;\text{and}\;\textbf{w}$ are said to be linearly dependent if one of the vectors is a linear combination of the other two. For instance, there exist two nonzero real numbers $\alpha$ and $β$ such that $\textbf{w}=\alpha \textbf{u}+β\textbf{v}.$ Otherwise, the vectors are called linearly independent. Show that $\textbf{u},\textbf{v},\;\text{and}\;\textbf{w}$ are coplanar if and only if they are linear dependent.

answer.solution: The vectors are coplanar exactly when the parallelepiped they span has volume 0, that is, when $\mathbf{u}\cdot(\mathbf{v}\times\mathbf{w})=0.$ If $\mathbf{w}=\alpha\mathbf{u}+\beta\mathbf{v},$ then $\mathbf{v}\times\mathbf{w}=\alpha(\mathbf{v}\times\mathbf{u})+\beta(\mathbf{v}\times\mathbf{v})=\alpha(\mathbf{v}\times\mathbf{u}),$ which is orthogonal to $\mathbf{u},$ so the triple scalar product is 0 and the vectors are coplanar. Conversely, suppose they are coplanar. If $\mathbf{u}$ and $\mathbf{v}$ are parallel, $\mathbf{v}=\lambda\mathbf{u}$ is already a linear combination of the others. Otherwise $\mathbf{u}$ and $\mathbf{v}$ are adjacent sides of a parallelogram in their plane, and $\mathbf{w},$ lying in that plane, is the diagonal of the parallelogram with sides along $\mathbf{u}$ and $\mathbf{v}$ that reaches its head: $\mathbf{w}=\alpha\mathbf{u}+\beta\mathbf{v}.$ Either way the vectors are linearly dependent.

exercises.prompt: Consider points $A(0,0,2),$ $B(1,0,2),$ $C(1,1,2),$ and $D(0,1,2).$ Are vectors $\kAB,$ $\kAC,$ and $\kAD$ linearly dependent (that is, one of the vectors is a linear combination of the other two)?

Show that vectors $\textbf{i}+\textbf{j},$ $\textbf{i}-\textbf{j},$ and $\textbf{i}+\textbf{j}+\textbf{k}$ are linearly independent—that is, there do not exist two nonzero real numbers $\alpha$ and $β$ such that $\textbf{i}+\textbf{j}+\textbf{k}=\alpha (\textbf{i}+\textbf{j})+β(\textbf{i}-\textbf{j}).$

answer.solution: Any combination $\alpha(\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j})+\beta(\mathbf{i}-\mathbf{j})=(\alpha+\beta)\mathbf{i}+(\alpha-\beta)\mathbf{j}$ has $\mathbf{k}$-component 0, while $\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j}+\mathbf{k}$ has $\mathbf{k}$-component 1. So no real $\alpha$ and $\beta$ give $\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j}+\mathbf{k},$ and the three vectors are linearly independent. Equivalently, their triple scalar product $\begin{vmatrix}1&1&0\\1&-1&0\\1&1&1\end{vmatrix}=-2\ne 0.$

exercises.prompt:
Let $\textbf{u}=\langle u_{1},u_{2}\rangle$ and $\textbf{v}=\langle v_{1},v_{2}\rangle$ be two-dimensional vectors. The cross product of vectors $\textbf{u}$ and $\textbf{v}$ is not defined. However, if the vectors are regarded as the three-dimensional vectors $\tilde{\textbf{u}}=\langle u_{1},u_{2},0\rangle$ and $\tilde{\textbf{v}}=\langle v_{1},v_{2},0\rangle ,$ respectively, then, in this case, we can define the cross product of $\tilde{\textbf{u}}$ and $\tilde{\textbf{v}}.$ In particular, in determinant notation, the cross product of $\tilde{\textbf{u}}$ and $\tilde{\textbf{v}}$ is given by

$$\tilde{\textbf{u}}\;\times \;\tilde{\textbf{v}}=\left|\begin{array}{lll}\textbf{i} & \textbf{j} & \textbf{k} \\ u_{1} & u_{2} & 0 \\ v_{1} & v_{2} & 0\end{array}\right|.$$

Use this result to compute $(\textbf{i}\cos \theta +\textbf{j}\sin \theta )\;\times \;(\textbf{i}\sin\theta -\textbf{j}\cos\theta ),$ where $\theta$ is a real number.
Determine a vector of magnitude $10$ perpendicular to the plane passing through the x-axis and point $P(1,2,4).$

Consider $\textbf{u}$ and $\textbf{v}$ two three-dimensional vectors. If the magnitude of the cross product vector $\textbf{u}\;\times \;\textbf{v}$ is $k$ times larger than the magnitude of vector $\textbf{u},$ show that the magnitude of $\textbf{v}$ is greater than or equal to $k,$ where $k$ is a natural number.

answer.solution: Let $\theta$ be the angle between $\mathbf{u}$ and $\mathbf{v}$ (with $\mathbf{u}\ne\mathbf{0}$). From $\|\mathbf{u}\times\mathbf{v}\|=k\|\mathbf{u}\|$ and $\|\mathbf{u}\times\mathbf{v}\|=\|\mathbf{u}\|\|\mathbf{v}\|\sin\theta$ we get $\|\mathbf{v}\|\sin\theta=k.$ Since $0\le\sin\theta\le 1,$ $\|\mathbf{v}\|\ge\|\mathbf{v}\|\sin\theta=k.$

exercises.prompt:
For the following exercises, determine whether the statement is true or false. Justify the answer with a proof or a counterexample.

For vectors $\textbf{a}$ and $\textbf{b}$ and any given scalar $c,$ $c(\textbf{a}\;\times \;\textbf{b})=(c\textbf{a})\;\times \;\textbf{b}.$

answer.solution: True. With $\mathbf{a}=\langle a_{1},a_{2},a_{3}\rangle$ and $\mathbf{b}=\langle b_{1},b_{2},b_{3}\rangle,$ each component of $(c\mathbf{a})\times\mathbf{b}$ is a difference of two products, each with one factor $ca_{i},$ for instance $(ca_{2})b_{3}-(ca_{3})b_{2}=c(a_{2}b_{3}-a_{3}b_{2}),$ which is $c$ times the corresponding component of $\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}.$ So $(c\mathbf{a})\times\mathbf{b}=c(\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}),$ as property iii. of the cross product states.
